nameStory: Dendrothele nivosa gets its species name 'nivosa' from the Latin word for 'snowy,' referring to its distinctive white, frost-like appearance when growing on wood. The genus name 'Dendrothele' combines Greek words meaning 'tree' and 'nipple,' describing how these small fungi form nipple-like bumps on tree bark and dead wood.
description: Dendrothele nivosa is a tiny crust fungus that forms thin, white patches on dead hardwood branches and logs. Rather than having the typical mushroom shape with cap and stem, this species grows as a flat, crusty coating that's peppered with small bumps or tubercles. Individual patches rarely exceed a few inches across, but multiple colonies can cover large sections of a fallen branch, creating striking white patches that look almost like someone splattered white paint on the wood.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Forms a thin white crust dotted with tiny raised bumps (tubercles) that feel slightly rough to the touch, like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright white when fresh, becoming cream-colored or slightly yellowish with age

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Spreads as thin patches directly on wood surface, never forming typical mushroom shapes

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found on dead hardwood, particularly favoring oak, maple, and birch branches

idTips.label: Texture When Dry
idTips.description: Becomes brittle and papery when dry, easily flaking off with a fingernail

habitat: Look for this species on fallen hardwood branches and small logs in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. It particularly favors oak, maple, and birch wood that's been dead for at least a year but hasn't completely decomposed. You'll often find it in shaded areas under the forest canopy where moisture levels remain more consistent.

seasonality.spring: Fresh white patches begin appearing on dead wood as moisture returns to the forest. This is an excellent time to spot the bright white coloration.
seasonality.summer: Continues growing and spreading during humid periods, though may become less noticeable during dry spells when it shrinks and becomes brittle.
seasonality.fall: Often most abundant after fall rains, with both fresh white patches and older cream-colored specimens visible on the same piece of wood.
seasonality.winter: Persists through winter but becomes dormant and papery. Snow cover makes it nearly impossible to spot during snowy periods.

funFact: Despite being tiny and inconspicuous, Dendrothele nivosa plays a crucial role as a 'pioneer decomposer' - it's often one of the very first fungi to colonize freshly fallen hardwood branches, beginning the slow process of returning dead wood back to soil nutrients.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with white slime molds or even bird droppings when small. However, slime molds are usually more irregular and slimy when fresh, while Dendrothele has those distinctive tiny raised bumps and a consistently crusty texture. The regular pattern of small tubercles is your best clue - bird droppings and slime molds don't have this organized bumpy texture.
contextualKnowledge: **WARNING: The limited observation data for this species in New England (94 records) suggests it may be either genuinely uncommon or frequently overlooked due to its small size and inconspicuous nature. This information is based on general knowledge of the genus, so some details should be verified with local experts.**
compareHints: Dendrothele nivosa is distinguished from its close relative Dendrothele acerina primarily by substrate preference - acerina typically grows on maple (Acer) species specifically, while nivosa is found on a broader range of hardwoods. The tubercles on nivosa also tend to be slightly more prominent and regularly spaced compared to acerina's more scattered, flatter bumps.
